title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid growth of artificial intelligence in higher education research and asks what the overall evidence-synthesis literature says about the scope, methods, quality, application areas, benefits, challenges, and gaps in this field. Rather than reviewing primary studies directly, the authors conduct a tertiary review, synthesising prior secondary research on AI in formal higher and continuing education. The paper is motivated by the recent surge in public and policy interest in AI, including generative AI, and argues that the field needs stronger conceptual, ethical, and methodological foundations.

The approach is a meta systematic review of reviews. The authors searched major databases and platforms, applied explicit inclusion criteria, and identified 66 evidence syntheses focused solely on higher or continuing education, published in English between 2018 and July 2023. They coded publication characteristics, author affiliations, review methods, quality indicators, thematic AI focus, participant contexts, key findings, benefits, challenges, and research gaps. The synthesis is organised partly around Zawacki-Richter et al.'s AI in education typology: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems and personalisation.

The population and context are not a single participant sample but the higher education evidence base itself. Included reviews concerned undergraduates, graduate learners, continuing education/adult learners, and institutional stakeholders such as students, educators, and administrators in formal higher education settings. The paper specifically excludes reviews focused only on generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, treating those as a newer stage of AI development.

The main conclusions are that AI in higher education review literature is dominated by systematic reviews, with major attention to general AI applications, profiling and prediction, and adaptive/personalised systems. Key findings across reviews suggest strong emphasis on adaptive systems, personalisation, and predictive uses, while intelligent tutoring systems and assessment-focused reviews are less common. The authors conclude that the field needs more ethical attention, stronger methodological rigour, better reporting, more interdisciplinary and international collaboration, and greater sensitivity to context. They also note uneven quality across reviews, limited use of quality appraisal, and underreporting of methods such as inter-rater reliability and data extraction procedures.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-systematic review of 66 evidence syntheses with explicit search, screening, and quality-appraisal methods, which is stronger than a single observational study. However, it is not a direct meta-analysis of primary effects and it focuses on higher education broadly rather than a tightly specified intervention-outcome estimate, so some relevance and synthesis limitations remain.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper documents broad but mixed institutional and implementation implications rather than a quantified causal impact on learners, and it reports no pooled effect sizes. As a result, overall impact is important but unclear rather than demonstrably positive at a medium or large magnitude.

interventions.use_case: Tertiary review synthesizing higher-education evidence reviews on AI-enabled adaptive systems and personalization, including personalized content delivery, learning paths, and recommender systems.
Review-of-reviews of profiling and prediction applications that use student data for dropout, retention, performance prediction, and institutional decision support.
Synthesis of review literature on AI for assessment and evaluation, including automated grading, feedback, and academic integrity uses in higher education.
Meta-systematic review covering prior higher-education review evidence on intelligent tutoring systems that diagnose learner needs and provide personalized instructional support.

finding.finding_summary: Across 66 higher-education evidence syntheses, the review found AIHEd research concentrated on general AI applications (47.0%) and profiling/prediction (28.8%), while key findings across reviews suggested the predominance of adaptive systems and personalization in practice. The paper reports substantial methodological and ethical gaps—especially around ethics, collaboration, quality appraisal, and contextual rigor—so institutional implications are promising but uneven and under-governed rather than clearly beneficial overall.
finding.measure: Distribution of review foci, publication/review characteristics, reported benefits/challenges/gaps, and institutional/application themes across included evidence syntheses

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates AI applications in higher education are used for administrative and academic-support efficiencies, including admissions, course scheduling, library services, quality assurance, automated assessment, and recommendation systems. However, only 39.3% of included reviews addressed institutional/administrative services, and the paper does not report pooled efficiency gains or comparable effect sizes, so evidence on actual productivity improvement remains suggestive rather than conclusive.
finding.measure: Reported administrative/instructional AI use cases such as scheduling, recommendation, quality assurance, and automated assessment in included reviews

finding.finding_summary: Within the synthesized review literature, some adaptive-system and chatbot studies reported benefits for affective outcomes such as reduced anxiety, satisfaction, and engagement, especially in language-learning and support contexts. At the same time, the authors emphasize that affective and social impacts remain under-evaluated, with reviews repeatedly calling for stronger evidence on motivation, engagement, and emotional dimensions of AI use.
finding.measure: Engagement, anxiety, satisfaction, emotion detection, and related affective/social outcomes reported in underlying reviews
